opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of those things where, in hindsight, we'll look back and realize a lot of the machinery we built into deep RL was a product of the hardware and the software constraints of the time, rather than something fundamental about the learning problem itself.

If you go back to DQN, the replay buffer and the target network were introduced for very good reasons. You had a single environment running on a CPU, producing highly correlated data, and if you just did naive online Q-learning with a neural network, it would diverge. So the replay buffer decorrelates the data, and the target network stabilizes the bootstrapping target. Those were clever fixes, but they come with real costs. The replay buffer takes a lot of memory, it makes you off-policy by construction, and it really complicates the whole system. The target network slows down learning, because you're always chasing a stale version of your own estimate.

What we found with work like PQN is that if you look at this through the lens of the theory, the instability in TD learning with function approximation can actually be addressed fairly directly with regularization, things like LayerNorm and some L2. That gives you a much more stable learning signal, so you no longer need a target network to stop things from blowing up. Then, if you run lots of environments in parallel, which you can now do on the GPU with frameworks in JAX, you get decorrelated data for free, just from the breadth of the parallel rollouts. So the replay buffer becomes optional rather than essential.

Why does this matter for the future? A few reasons. One is simplicity. Simpler algorithms are easier to understand, easier to analyze, and easier to build on. When you have fewer moving parts, the community can actually figure out what's doing the work. Second is speed. If your whole pipeline, environment and agent, lives on the accelerator, and you're not shuffling data in and out of a giant buffer, you can get orders-of-magnitude speedups. That changes the kind of science you can do. You can run many seeds, sweep hyperparameters properly, do meta-learning over the algorithms themselves. I think a lot of the reproducibility problems in RL come from people just not being able to afford enough runs.

And third, it opens the door back to online, on-policy-style value-based methods, which I think connect more naturally to things like large-scale training of foundation models, where you want something that is stable, scalable, and plays well with massive parallelism.

I don't want to overclaim. There will still be settings, sample-limited ones, real-world robotics, where reusing data via a buffer is extremely valuable. But I think the broader lesson is that we should constantly revisit our assumptions when the hardware changes. A lot of what we thought was necessary turns out to be just a workaround, and once you remove it, you often get algorithms that are both simpler and better.

r001.rationale: The response says removing the target network and making replay optional can yield simpler algorithms that are easier to understand.

r002.rationale: It links stability to regularization and understandability to simplicity, but does not say that greater understandability makes the algorithms more robust.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So I think the honest framing is that target networks and replay buffers were never really part of the theory of reinforcement learning. They were patches. When DQN came out, you had this beautiful idea of doing Q-learning with a deep network, and it just didn't work out of the box. It diverged. And the fixes were, okay, let's freeze a copy of the network so the bootstrapping target stops chasing itself, and let's store experience and sample it randomly so the gradient updates look more like i.i.d. supervised learning. Both of those are engineering workarounds for the fact that we were trying to force a method with convergence guarantees in the tabular, linear setting onto function approximators that it was never designed for.

So the question I find interesting isn't really "can we delete these two components." It's "what were they compensating for, and can we address that directly." And I think the answer is yes, and that's what's exciting. If you look at the recent work on things like cross-Q, or on regularisation and normalisation schemes, or on parallel environments where you get massive batches of fresh on-policy-ish data, you can actually stabilise temporal difference learning without the target network, and in many cases without a huge replay buffer. And once you do that, a few things happen.

The first is simplicity, which people underrate. Every one of these components introduces hyperparameters. Target update period, replay ratio, buffer size, prioritisation exponents. Each one is a knob that someone has to tune, and each one is an interaction effect with every other knob. If you can remove them, the algorithm gets more robust, more reproducible, and frankly more honest, because a lot of what gets reported as algorithmic progress in RL is actually hyperparameter search.

The second is speed, in a very concrete sense. Target networks slow down learning. They're a deliberate lag. You're saying, I don't trust my current estimate, so I'm going to bootstrap off a stale one. If you can trust your current estimate, you propagate value information through time much faster. And replay buffers are, from a hardware perspective, a bottleneck. We now have simulators that run entirely on accelerators, millions of steps per second. In that regime, storing and sampling experience from a buffer becomes the thing you're waiting on, not the environment. So getting rid of it is almost required if we want to take advantage of where compute is going.

And the third, which I think is the deepest, is about what kind of learning we want to do. Replay is fundamentally about reusing old data, and old data is off-policy. The gap between on-policy and off-policy learning has been one of the central tensions in the field for decades. If we can learn stably and sample efficiently from very recent, very abundant data, we're in a different regime altogether, and a lot of the theoretical headaches just go away, because you're closer to the setting where the methods actually have guarantees.

Now, I want to be careful. I don't think these components disappear everywhere. If you're in a setting where data is genuinely expensive, robotics, healthcare, anything where you can't simulate, then reusing experience is not a convenience, it's the whole game. Offline RL is basically "replay buffer as the entire dataset." So I don't see this as "replay is dead." I see it as a bifurcation. In the simulation-rich, compute-rich regime, we strip the algorithms down to something much closer to plain TD learning with good architectural choices, and we lean on scale. In the data-poor regime, we lean even harder on reuse, but we do it with methods designed for off-policy data from the start, rather than pretending it's on-policy by shuffling it.

The thing I'd hope for in the long run is that we end up with algorithms where stability comes from understanding, not from scaffolding. If you'd asked someone in 2015 why the target network works, you'd have gotten a hand-wavy answer about moving targets. We're now at the point where we can say something precise about the optimisation dynamics, and once you can say something precise, you can design for it. That, to me, is what the removal of these components really signals. Not that we've found a trick that lets us drop them, but that we're finally starting to understand the thing we were patching over.

r001.rationale: The candidate hopes for algorithms whose stability comes from understanding rather than scaffolding, and presents removing these components as a signal of that growing understanding.

r002.rationale: It says removing components can make algorithms more robust and separately says stability should come from understanding, but does not clearly connect greater understandability to greater robustness.

astra-6.text:
I think the exciting possibility is that we can make reinforcement learning much more genuinely online. Replay buffers let you reuse experience, and target networks help stabilise learning, but they also introduce machinery that can make it harder to understand the underlying learning dynamics.

If we can get stability without those components, we could have algorithms that learn from each transition as it arrives and adapt more quickly when things change. That’s particularly interesting in multi-agent settings, where other agents are learning too, so old experience can become misleading.

But removing them isn’t itself the goal. You still have to explain what prevents divergence, and how you recover the sample efficiency that replay gives you. Otherwise, you may just be trading a memory cost for a much larger interaction cost.

So I’d see this as an opportunity to revisit the foundations: can we design the update rule so that stable learning is a property of the algorithm itself? If we can, that could give us a simpler and more useful building block for continual learning.

r001.rationale: The response says removing these components could reduce machinery that obscures learning dynamics and lead to a simpler algorithm, expressing hope for greater understandability.

r002.rationale: The response discusses stability and understandability separately, but does not say that greater understandability would make the algorithms more robust.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the exciting possibility is that we could make reinforcement learning much more genuinely online. Replay buffers let us reuse experience, and target networks help stabilize learning, but they also introduce quite a lot of machinery. If we can understand how to get stable learning without them, that could lead to simpler algorithms that adapt more quickly as the environment changes.

But removing them isn’t itself the objective. You still have to deal with correlated observations, bootstrapping, and the fact that your data distribution changes as your policy changes. And if you throw away replay, you need to ask what happens to sample efficiency. So the interesting question is: what mechanism replaces the role those components were playing?

For me, the bigger opportunity is a better understanding of the learning dynamics. If that understanding gives us methods that are stable, efficient, and less dependent on these additional components, then it could change how we design reinforcement learning algorithms.

r001.rationale: The response hopes for simpler algorithms and better understanding of learning dynamics, but does not clearly say that eliminating these components will make the algorithms themselves more understandable.

r002.rationale: It links better understanding of learning dynamics to methods that are stable, but does not state that making algorithms more understandable can make them more robust.
